cards.front: Why does one sponsor workshop not complete discovery?
cards.back: **Discovery is elicitation across roles**, not one sponsor workshop. The sponsor brings the literal ask, but the people who do the work and the data owners hold what that workshop misses: the baseline, the real job and the constraints that eliminate designs (trap: T-SKIPDISC, Build Before Agreeing).

cards.front: In discovery, what do the people who do the work supply, and what do the data owners supply?
cards.back: **The people who do the work hold the baseline** and often show that the real job differs from the literal ask. **The data owners hold the constraints that eliminate designs.** Discovery that skips either group leaves the baseline or the binding constraint unknown.

cards.front: Interviews show the real job differs from the sponsor's literal ask. Who makes the reframe, and what is your part?
cards.back: **The sponsor makes the reframe; you bring them the evidence of the underlying job.** Building the literal ask regardless, or quietly building your own version instead, takes that decision from its owner (trap: T-OWNER, Deciding for the Owner).

cards.front: What is the current-process baseline, and what does it make possible?
cards.back: **Today's workflow measured under one agreed definition**, for example cycle time, error rate and cost per unit. Without it, no target, pilot result or ROI claim can be judged, because each one is a comparison against it.

cards.front: Two systems calculate cost per claim differently and no current figure is recorded. What must happen before design starts?
cards.back: **Baseline today's workflow under one agreed definition.** An eval harness's first scores cannot stand in, because the baseline is measured on today's process, not the new system (trap: T-LATER, Right Answer, Wrong Time). The baseline comes before the target, since the target is stated against it.

cards.front: What separates a goal such as 'a better claims experience' from a measurable target?
cards.back: **A measurable target is a number stated against the baseline and signed by the owner.** 'A better claims experience' names a direction but gives a pilot result nothing to be tested against, so it is a goal, not a target.

cards.front: Discovery notes record the goal 'faster, cheaper claims handling'. What is your part in making it measurable, and who sets the number?
cards.back: **You propose candidate targets drawn from the baseline; the owner sets and signs the number**, before design starts. Writing in a figure of your own, even one anchored to the baseline, decides for the owner (trap: T-OWNER, Deciding for the Owner).

cards.front: Name the six kinds of limit a constraint inventory lists.
cards.back: **Latency, cost ceiling, residency, compliance regime, data access and integration limits.** Find the binding one, the constraint that eliminates designs, before any model or design is chosen.

cards.front: Which three questions usually surface the binding constraint in discovery?
cards.back: **Where does the data live, who may see it, and which decisions does a regulator expect a person to make?** Ask them before shortlisting or benchmarking models; benchmarking first is good practice at the wrong time (trap: T-LATER, Right Answer, Wrong Time).

cards.front: What three facts does a data and access map record for each input?
cards.back: **Which system holds it, who owns it, and under whose identity it can be read.** A design that relies on access nobody has granted rests on an unstated assumption, and the map exposes it before build (trap: T-ASSUME, Unstated Assumption).

cards.front: Two executives both expect to approve go-live. What kind of problem is this, and when is it settled?
cards.back: **It is an open discovery item**, settled now by naming exactly one decision owner, not a detail to sort out at launch. Each decision (success criteria, risk acceptance, go/no-go) needs exactly one named owner.

cards.front: A residency constraint nobody raised in discovery surfaces midway through design. What is the right move?
cards.back: **Go back to the owner of that constraint** and resolve it with them, instead of patching the design around it. A late constraint means a role or data owner was not asked, so the fix is targeted discovery, not a workaround.

cards.front: How does handling a new scope request after sign-off differ from handling a constraint that surfaced late?
cards.back: **A new scope request goes to the decision owner as a scope decision**, rather than reopening discovery wholesale. A late constraint instead goes back to the role or data owner who was not asked, for that constraint, rather than being patched around (trap: T-OWNER, Deciding for the Owner).

cards.front: Regulated or sensitive data is in scope. Who joins discovery beyond users, data owners and engineering?
cards.back: **Legal, security, and privacy or compliance.** Stakeholders map to the risk in scope, and these roles hold constraints that eliminate designs, so sending them a finished architecture for sign-off comes too late (trap: T-SKIPDISC).

cards.front: When capturing the as-is process, what must discovery record that no document holds?
cards.back: **The tacit checks experts apply** that no document records. They are part of the real job, so a design built only from the written process would leave them out.

cards.front: Which three questions about errors should discovery ask, and what do the answers drive?
cards.back: **What does an error cost, who bears it, and how would anyone notice?** The answers drive autonomy and review design: how much the system may do alone and where a person reviews its work.

cards.front: A requirement cannot be traced to any stakeholder statement. What do you do with it?
cards.back: **Log it as an assumption with an owner.** Every requirement should trace to a stakeholder statement; one that does not is an assumption until its owner confirms it, not something the design may silently rely on.

cards.front: What is an operating point, and who chooses it?
cards.back: **One position on the curve that trades accuracy against cost, latency and review load.** You show the curve and what each point means; the accountable owner picks the point (trap: T-OWNER, Deciding for the Owner).

cards.front: Which trade-offs go to the accountable owner, and when may the architect settle one alone?
cards.back: **Any trade-off stakeholders can see goes to the owner**, such as the operating point. You settle one alone only when the owner has explicitly delegated it, or it is an implementation detail with no trade-off stakeholders can see (the exception in trap: T-OWNER, Deciding for the Owner).

cards.front: How do you turn an accuracy percentage into something an executive can weigh?
cards.back: **Convert it into an error count per month by case type.** At 14,000 claims a month, 99.7 percent still means about 42 misroutes, and the executive can weigh which claim types they fall in and what each costs. Never promise, refuse or quietly redefine the number (trap: T-OVERPROMISE, Reassuring Guarantee).

cards.front: Why state the cost of reversal for each option you present to an owner?
cards.back: **It sets how much evidence the decision needs.** A choice that is cheap to undo can be made on thinner evidence than one that locks in a region, a vendor or a contract.

cards.front: Executives decide whether. Name the four things their artefact carries.
cards.back: **Decision, impact, risk and the ask**, with impact in metrics they already track. They are deciding whether, not approving how, so implementation detail such as chunking or prompt design is the wrong artefact for them (trap: T-AUDIENCE, Wrong Artefact).

cards.front: Beyond the architecture and data flows, what three things do security reviewers need?
cards.back: **The privilege model, the injection posture and the blast radius.** Security and platform reviewers approve how the system works, so for them the architecture view is the right artefact, not an executive brief.

cards.front: Why report pilot results by segment rather than as one aggregate?
cards.back: **An aggregate that clears the bar can hide a failing slice.** An owner deciding on the overall figure alone cannot see where the system falls short, so results go to them segmented, with the method stated (trap: T-AGGREGATE, Average Hides Slice).

cards.front: What must accompany segmented pilot results before a sceptical finance owner will credit the numbers?
cards.back: **The method, stated alongside the results.** A sceptical finance owner discounts any number whose method is missing, however well it clears the bar, so segmented results are reported with how they were measured.

cards.front: A pilot misses its agreed bar. Name three bounded options you might bring the owner.
cards.back: **Human review on the failing slice, a narrower scope, or more build time**, each with its cost. Present them alongside the gap by slice so the owner chooses with the evidence in front of them.

cards.front: After a missed pilot bar, whose call is lowering the bar or cancelling, and whose is reporting a different metric that passes?
cards.back: **Lowering the bar or cancelling is the owner's call; quietly reporting a different metric that passes is nobody's.** Swapping in any yardstick the pilot happens to pass hides the miss from the person who must decide (trap: T-OWNER, Deciding for the Owner).

cards.front: What three things does 'recommend; do not abdicate' require you to put in front of the owner?
cards.back: **The options, your recommendation, and the condition that would reverse it.** The recommendation informs the choice rather than making it: the owner still sees every option's trade-off in full and decides.

cards.front: Two peer stakeholders disagree on an operating point and nobody owns the decision. Who decides?
cards.back: **The sponsor**, once you have shown the measured trade-off: escalate when no single accountable owner exists, then record the decision. Splitting the difference or building both variants decides for them (trap: T-OWNER).

cards.front: How does a design review run as a decision meeting differ from a walkthrough?
cards.back: **A decision meeting puts each open decision to its owner**; a walkthrough only presents the design. The review should end with owned, recorded decisions, not just a shared understanding of how the system works.

cards.front: What is an error budget, and what does it make of 'the model will sometimes be wrong'?
cards.back: **The amount of failure the SLA tolerates in a period.** It turns 'the model will sometimes be wrong' from a concession into a managed quantity, with a defined response when the budget is spent.

cards.front: An SLA draft states average latency and excludes surge days. How should latency be stated instead?
cards.back: **As a percentile measured at peak, with what peak includes written down.** For Meridian, peak includes catastrophe surges: an average or a surge exclusion hides exactly the hours claimants feel (trap: T-AVGSLA, SLA on Averages).

cards.front: Why must a latency clause say whether it means time to first token or completion?
cards.back: **Streaming improves the wait users perceive, not completion time.** So time to first token can improve while completion time stays the same, and a clause that does not say which wait it means leaves the commitment ambiguous.

cards.front: What comes before any latency or quality number is written into an SLA?
cards.back: **A measured baseline that includes peak, plus agreement on which wait and what counts as an error.** Each threshold is derived from its source, so a percentile clause or error budget drafted before the baseline is right in shape but premature (trap: T-LATER, Right Answer, Wrong Time).

cards.front: What method must accompany an accuracy floor for it to be enforceable?
cards.back: **A named, versioned eval set drawn from production, an agreed grader checked against human labels, and a sample size.** A floor without a method cannot be breached, so it cannot be enforced (trap: T-VIBES, Number Without Bar).

cards.front: What does a degraded-mode definition specify?
cards.back: **What happens when the error budget is spent or a dependency fails**, such as a queue, a fallback or a human handoff, and which remedy the customer receives. It is defined in advance, not improvised during the failure.

cards.front: Why can't your SLA simply adopt your model provider's availability SLA?
cards.back: **A provider's SLA covers only one dependency.** What you commit is composed from every serial dependency's availability plus your own behaviour, so it cannot exceed their product without redundancy or a degraded path.

cards.front: Where does each SLA threshold come from: availability, latency and quality?
cards.back: **Availability from business criticality and the cost of downtime, latency from the discovery UX requirement, and quality from the eval acceptance bar.** Each number is derived from its source rather than chosen to sound strict.

cards.front: Every override is captured on a dashboard, but nobody has opened it since launch. What does the feedback loop lack?
cards.back: **A pre-agreed review trigger, a named owner who must act, and a path that turns confirmed failures into eval cases.** The signal already exists, and a dashboard nobody owns is an open loop; adding more ratings only feeds it (trap: T-VIBES, Number Without Bar).

cards.front: Someone has implied the system never errs. What must the correction contain, and when should it happen?
cards.back: **The measured rate, the review path and the remedy, in writing, now.** Correcting it before the first visible failure means that failure lands as an expected, handled event rather than a trust incident (trap: T-OVERPROMISE, Reassuring Guarantee).

cards.front: What can an honest commitment guarantee outright, and what must it state as a measured rate?
cards.back: **A deterministic control you own can be guaranteed**, such as code enforcing a limit or a human approving every payment. Model output is probabilistic, so it gets a measured rate, a review path and a remedy, never deterministic correctness (trap: T-OVERPROMISE, Reassuring Guarantee).

cards.front: Name the three items that keep an SLA current after it is signed.
cards.back: **An owner, a review cadence and a renegotiation trigger**, such as a change in scope, traffic mix or regulation. The trigger names the change that reopens the commitment, so the SLA is revisited when its basis shifts rather than left to drift.

cards.front: A new requirement arrives mid-build. What happens to it before and after the sponsor accepts it?
cards.back: **An impact assessment against the agreed scope first, then formal re-baselining once accepted.** The assessment covers cost, date, risk and the eval set; the sponsor decides; an accepted change goes through design and the eval gate.

cards.front: Why are quietly absorbing a new requirement and refusing it outright equally wrong?
cards.back: **Both decide for the owner.** Absorbing hides a cost, date or risk change from the sponsor, and refusing withholds a choice that is theirs. Change control puts the impact assessment in front of the sponsor instead (trap: T-OWNER).

cards.front: Name documentation's three readers and what each one needs.
cards.back: **The executive needs the decision and its impact, the reviewer must approve the design, and the engineer will operate or change it.** Each needs a different artefact, so documentation is fitted to the reader rather than written once for everyone (trap: T-AUDIENCE, Wrong Artefact).

cards.front: Which decisions warrant an ADR?
cards.back: **Any decision that is costly to reverse or likely to be questioned.** The ADR records the reasoning, including why each rejected alternative lost, so a team weighing a change can check it instead of re-choosing an option that already lost.

cards.front: EU residency rules out global cross-Region routing. Why must the ADR record that forcing constraint?
cards.back: **So a future team can check whether the constraint still holds.** Residency forced in-region or geography-bound Bedrock endpoints because global cross-Region routing does not guarantee location; if the constraint lapses, the decision can be reopened on evidence.

cards.front: What is an ADR's revisit trigger, and what extra item does an ADR for a vendor dependency state?
cards.back: **The revisit trigger is the condition that reopens the decision.** For a vendor dependency the ADR also states the exit cost, so lock-in becomes an owned decision rather than an accident.

cards.front: A decision recorded in an ADR is being changed. How do you update the record?
cards.back: **Write a new ADR that supersedes and cites the old one**, rather than editing it. Kept in version control beside the code, the chain of ADRs preserves the history of why the system changed.

cards.front: Name the four contents of implementation guidance for a team that builds without you.
cards.back: **Interfaces, the prompt and tool inventory with versions, eval thresholds as acceptance criteria, and known failure modes with their handling.** Together they let the team build and judge when it is done without asking the architect.

cards.front: Besides listing known limitations, what must a handoff attach to each one?
cards.back: **An escalation path.** The known limitations form the failure-mode register, and pairing each with its escalation path tells the operating team what the system cannot do and where each failure goes.

cards.front: Name the four parts of a runbook entry.
cards.back: **Symptom, likely cause, diagnostic step and action**, grounded in traces the team can actually query. The entry takes an operator from what they see to what they do, without its author in the room.

cards.front: Why does a runbook entry that says 'contact the architect' fail?
cards.back: **It transfers nothing**: the knowledge stays with one person, who will not always be there. A real entry points to a diagnostic step in traces the team can query, so the operator can act without the author.

cards.front: Why is a chat channel, named contact, recording or system prompt never the record?
cards.back: **Each holds only fragments of knowledge**: none survives staff turnover, and none records why the alternatives lost. A channel is fine for live coordination, but decisions and procedures need durable artefacts (trap: T-AUDIENCE, Wrong Artefact).

cards.front: A proposal reopens a past architecture decision whose only records are a meeting recording, code comments and a system prompt. What should the team produce?
cards.back: **A version-controlled ADR reconstructed with the people who remember**, including why the rejected option lost, then an assessment of the proposal as a superseding ADR. Rejecting it because the original team 'must have had reasons' assumes the old constraints still hold (trap: T-ASSUME).

cards.front: Name, in order, the seven lifecycle stages you place a stem on before reading the options.
cards.back: **Discovery, design, POC, pilot, production and handoff, monitoring, iteration.** Place the stem first because most distractors are correct actions for a neighbouring stage: good practice that is simply early or late (trap: T-LATER, Right Answer, Wrong Time).

cards.front: What do a POC's exit criteria test, compared with a pilot's?
cards.back: **A POC's criteria test feasibility on representative data; a pilot's test value with real users**, plus guardrail metrics that must not get worse. A POC that passes has shown feasibility, not value, and both sets are written and signed before the stage starts.

cards.front: What is a guardrail metric in a pilot's exit criteria?
cards.back: **A metric that must not get worse** while the pilot tests value with real users. It is agreed with the value measures before the stage starts, because criteria agreed after the results arrive are a story, not a gate.

cards.front: A pilot ended without exit criteria and nobody can say whether it worked. What is the first move?
cards.back: **Agree exit criteria with the owner first**, then retry with a defined scope and guardrail metrics. Rerunning or extending it unchanged would only produce another result nobody can judge.

cards.front: Name what production readiness adds that a pilot can skip.
cards.back: **SLOs, on-call, rollback, runbooks, and a named monitoring owner** who accepts the handoff in writing and watches for drift against the pilot baseline. Without them, the first production incident lands on nobody.

cards.front: The pilot passed and the owner approved production, but there is no rollback, on-call or accepted owner. What comes next?
cards.back: **Complete production readiness**: rollback, on-call, runbooks and a signed handoff to a named owner. Extending the pilot overrides an owner who already decided (trap: T-OWNER), and planning the next region closes none of the gaps (trap: T-LATER).

cards.front: What does a handoff transfer, beyond the files?
cards.back: **Capability**: the operating team must be able to diagnose from traces and run the eval suite without you. Documents the team cannot act on alone are not a handoff.

cards.front: The first incident after handoff lands. What is the architect's role?
cards.back: **Coach the operating team through it instead of fixing it for them.** Fixing it yourself keeps you as the permanent fixer and leaves the team no better able to handle the next incident.

cards.front: Which three changes send a live system back to discovery instead of iteration?
cards.back: **A changed use case, data source or regulatory regime**, because the constraints the design was built on no longer hold. When traces and per-slice evals instead point to a fixable component, you iterate. Swapping the model or re-architecting before reading that evidence is the trap (trap: T-OBSERVE, Fix Before Seeing).

cards.front: Why change only one thing at a time when iterating?
cards.back: **So the next reading can be attributed to that change.** Change the prompt and retrieval together and any improvement or regression cannot be pinned on either, so the evidence stops deciding the next step.

cards.front: Which four discovery outputs must be agreed before design starts, and where does the data and access map fit?
cards.back: **The current-process baseline, a measurable target, the constraint inventory and a named decision owner.** The data and access map, which some lists count as a fifth output, details the inventory's data-access limits. If any is missing, or came only from the sponsor, discovery is unfinished; once all are agreed, design is the next step (trap: T-SKIPDISC, Build Before Agreeing).

cards.front: Name the three outputs of the design phase.
cards.back: **An architecture traced to requirements, ADRs, and an eval plan with thresholds.** Those thresholds later serve as the acceptance criteria in the implementation guidance for the team that builds without you.

cards.front: What does each of handoff, monitoring and iteration output?
cards.back: **Handoff gives runbooks, the eval suite and a named owner; monitoring gives per-slice alerts and review triggers; iteration gives one attributable, eval-gated change.** Each lifecycle phase has its own outputs.

cards.front: Name the four steps of retirement, the phase that closes the lifecycle loop.
cards.back: **Notify users, migrate in-flight work and downstream dependents, dispose of data under the retention rules, and record why in an ADR.** Retirement closes the lifecycle loop rather than just switching the system off.

cards.front: Which four pilot assumptions must be re-checked before scaling it up?
cards.back: **Input mix, edge-case frequency, support load and cost at volume.** They rarely match the pilot's, so rolling out on the pilot's numbers rests on an assumption the stem must grant (trap: T-ASSUME, Unstated Assumption).

cards.front: Why is a no-go result against pre-agreed criteria counted as a success?
cards.back: **It saved the build**: the gate stopped an investment the evidence did not support. It is not a reason to rerun the pilot unchanged, because the criteria did exactly the job they were agreed for.

cards.front: After launch, technical targets are met but adoption lags. How do you diagnose it?
cards.back: **With user research and usage measured against the discovery success criteria.** Because the technical targets already pass, the question is how people use the system, and the success criteria agreed in discovery are the yardstick.

cards.front: After launch, what are the system's realised benefits reviewed against?
cards.back: **The business case.** Launch does not end the evaluation: realised benefits are checked against what the business case claimed, just as adoption is checked against the discovery success criteria.
